    Your cassette shelf

    Boombox field handbook

    Tap a key or switch. Drag knobs up/right to increase, down/left to decrease. Drag EQ sliders vertically; drag the tuner across its scale. Keyboard: Tab to a control, arrow keys to adjust, Enter or Space to press.

    Sets volume to 65%, turns power on and mute off, centers balance, restores stereo and normal speed, and resets tone/EQ boosts. Keeps your song, tape and position, then resumes playback.

    Controls on this boombox
    Listening to radio stations

    Open Radio to host a timed mixtape program or tune into another player’s station. Your boombox’s volume, EQ and mute affect your own audio. Use the host desk to pause, skip or change level for all listeners.

    Pause stops your monitor locally; Play rejoins the live program. The tuner returns to the live position. Choosing a song or cassette leaves the station. Hosts must check in every five minutes and keep their browser connected.

    Tapes, music & scenery

    Eject or tap the cassette door to open the shelf. Opening the deck pauses music. Insert a tape, close the deck, then press Play. Removing a tape empties the player.

    Music & tapes lets you upload MP3/WAV files, arrange songs into a mixtape and publish a cassette. Connect your profile to keep your collection.

    The workshop’s Test animation starts the illustration demo. Use Music & tapes or the boombox’s Play key for songs. Pause scene freezes scenery animation while music continues.

    In atmosphere mode, tap the boombox to zoom in. In boombox mode, tap Scene to zoom out. Front panel enlarges the controls; Full radio reveals the handle and antenna.

    If the sound goes quiet

    Check this handbook’s status first. Mute and volume zero silence sound; Power, Pause, Stop and Eject stop playback. Tuning seeks through the current song and can reach its end.

    Deep EQ cuts reduce some frequencies. Hard balance sends music to one side, and Mono can cancel parts of some stereo recordings. Restore sound returns these settings to a neutral starting point.

    If playback still cannot start, check your device volume and audio output, tap Play again, or select another song. Reconnect your profile if an uploaded song is unavailable.

    Connect a phone profile to keep your assigned frequency and host identity. You can tune into live stations below.

    01 / Station identity

    Three letters, your own frequency, and a DJ alter ego. The band and assigned frequency stay with your profile.

    02 / Your broadcast program

    Add up to five mixtapes in playing order. Uploaded songs are compressed in your browser for radio playback; your originals stay in your library. Programs support up to 100 songs, three hours total, and 40 MB of shared audio. Uploaded songs can be up to ten minutes each.

    Drop something on the airwaves

    Check in every five minutes. The slot cannot extend itself. Keep this browser connected: closing it or losing its heartbeat releases the slot within 90 seconds.

    Tuned in

    Boombox volume and EQ shape your own listening. The host controls the shared program. Resuming your audio rejoins the live position.

    03 / Tune the airwaves

    0 / 20 stations live

    How Atelier radio works

    These are virtual app frequencies, with 199 channels on each of eight bands. Each profile keeps one assigned frequency. Up to twenty profiles can broadcast at once.

    Everyone plays the same mixtape program against a shared clock. Music is played by each browser; host commands and sound effects arrive with a short delay. Uploaded songs are shared only through an active broadcast. This mode does not transmit your microphone.

    The robot announcer reads your three-letter station, band, frequency and chosen DJ name using a low-pitched browser voice. Its voice varies by device. If speech is unavailable, the station ID stays visible with a chime.

    ORIGINAL DESIGNS / VINTAGE SPIRIT / BUILT BY YOU

    On the workbench.

    The starting builds mix real vintage hardware cues with our own anime-inspired color and drawing choices.

    Your reference photos

    Silver Street borrows the RX-4930’s vertical dial and corner graphics. Broadcast King draws on the SZ-5100’s horn tweeters, chrome bridges and stacked decks. Lemon FM and Ghost Glow explore yellow-and-silver hardware and illuminated clear plastic.

    JVC RC-M90

    A broad, squared-off face, big woofers and smaller tweeters inform the Classic shell.

    JVC M-90 at MoMA

    Sharp GF-777

    Multiple large drivers, twin decks and a busy control panel inspire Double Impact.

    GF-777 reference & manual

    Sony & Panasonic

    The Sony CFS-99’s substantial single-deck form and Panasonic’s rounded Cobra-top era provide two more directions.

    Sony CFS-99 restoration
    Panasonic & ’90s models

    Street sound

    Radio Raheem’s boombox in Do the Right Thing (1989) is part of the film and hip-hop culture behind this workshop.

    The boombox at the Smithsonian

    Akira · 1988

    Our Neo Tokyo palette draws on red machinery, dark industrial details and the film’s future-city setting.

    Akira at the Academy

    Cowboy Bebop · 1998

    Space Jazz is our interpretation: worn teal, warm brass and a cassette that looks like it has traveled.

    Cowboy Bebop at Sunrise

    The presets are original interpretations, not replicas or official merchandise. Brand and film names identify research references. Wood cabinets and fictional speaker arrays are creative customization options.
